turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, I am so sorry we're late. Err, the garage was full, and then a school bus just sat on Maple Street forever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, truly. We still have the time. I'm Dr. Hale.
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. I'm Carla, his mom. This is Owen. He just turned seven.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. It is a pleasure to meet you.

[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Chart's updated. Weight 23 kilograms, temp thirty six point eight celsius. Umm, my sister's little boy had a total meltdown in that same garage last Tuesday, made us late to his checkup. Our circus, not yours.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Dana. What brings you in?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): My skin has been itching quite a lot, doctor.
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He's got these dry rough patches behind both knees and in the creases of his elbows. He scratches them, especially at night, till they look raw.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dry rough patches behind the knees and in the elbow creases, itchy, scratched raw, worse at night. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, about six weeks, maybe a little longer. I can't pin the day it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Any oozing or crusting? Any wheezing?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. Nothing oozing. And he has not wheezed.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Good, that's reassuring. Anyone at home with asthma or eczema?
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma. He keeps a blue inhaler in his bag. I don't have either. Nobody's told me Owen had eczema before.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Father with asthma, noted. What have you been putting on his skin?

[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The big white tub, we just call it the white cream, thick moisturizer, morning and night. A little pink tube, the steroid Dr. Patel gave last year, she said once a day, but uh I forget a lot of nights so it's more like a few times a week, and I cannot remember the real name of that pink one. And sometimes the blue lotion from the drugstore, just a plain moisturizer, if the white tub is upstairs.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. White moisturizer twice a day, an unnamed pink steroid that was supposed to be daily but often gets skipped, and a blue plain lotion now and then. Owen, may I look? Sleeves and pant legs up, please.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Certainly.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both elbow creases and the skin behind both knees have dry, slightly scaly patches. No honey-colored crust. The skin is not warm to the touch.
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He scratches in his sleep too. I find little spots of blood on the sheets some mornings.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): The itch comes from a leaky skin barrier. Water slips out, and the small nerves in the skin fire off, especially when he is warm under the blankets at night. That part is not an infection.
[SEG0022] person_4 (NURSE): Right. My own hands split every winter from the dish soap at my place. Drives me crazy. That's me, though, not Owen.

[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, that hail yesterday, did you see it? We pulled over by the ball field after school and just watched, little white pellets bouncing, and the coach was dragging a tarp over the bases like it was game seven.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): I counted forty hailstones, doctor, before mother said we ought to leave.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. I got caught between the lot and the door. My shoes are still damp.

[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the traffic after was ridiculous, everybody creeping along. We spent the whole ride on his class turtle. His name is Pickle. He will only eat the fancy lettuce, not the cheap kind.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pickle. Alright. Coming back to the skin.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, I think this is eczema, atopic dermatitis. That's my working read. I'm not proving it with a test today, and I don't think it's infected.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. So do we keep using the pink tube?

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to stop that unnamed pink steroid. We'll switch to triamcinalone zero point one percent cream, a thin layer on the patches only, twice a day for seven days, then stop.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day for a week, patches only. Got it. What about the white cream and the blue one?

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the white cream, but use it all over at least three times a day, especially within a few minutes after a short lukewarm bath. The blue lotion is fine as a backup when the white tub isn't around. Mild soap, pat dry, don't rub.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cotton pajamas if you have them, and keep his nails short so the scratching does less harm. Steroid stays off the face, and off any spot that's openly bleeding. Just moisturize those.

[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): White cream three times a day after lukewarm baths, blue one only as backup, triamcinalone on the patches twice a day for a week, stop the pink tube, short nails, no steroid on the face. Did I miss a piece?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the whole plan. Yes.
[SEG0036] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What if it doesn't settle?

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in three weeks either way, so I can recheck it. If the patches get hot, or there's pus, or he gets a fever before then, call and we'll see him sooner.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I appreciate your help.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll pick it up at the pharmacy. Thanks for squeezing us in after we were late.
[SEG0040] person_4 (NURSE): I'll send the triamcinalone to the pharmacy now.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sounds good. See you in three weeks, Owen.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Oozing denied; crusting denied only on exam as honey-colored crust, not by family member.
bad.text: Oozing or crusting (status=absent, assertion=negative, reported_by=family_member, temporality=current)

bad.reason: Supposed to be once daily, but actual use is only a few times a week.
bad.text: pink steroid tube (frequency=once a day, status=currently_used, reported_by=family_member)

omissions.text: Current pink steroid tube is not actually being used once daily; it was prescribed once a day but is being applied only a few times a week because doses are often missed.
No one has previously told the mother that Owen had eczema before.
Doctor stated that eczema/atopic dermatitis was a working diagnosis and was not being proven with a test today.
The white cream should be applied especially within a few minutes after a short lukewarm bath.
Steroid should be kept off any spots that are openly bleeding; those areas should be moisturized only.
If concerning changes occur before the 3-week review, the instruction was to call and they would see him sooner.
Triamcinolone prescription was to be sent to the pharmacy.
